analysis.one_liner: Requires voter-verified paper ballots for federal elections and mandatory surprise hand-count audits of results.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, never received a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for federal elections. Every vote would have to be cast on a durable paper ballot the voter could check before it was counted, that paper ballot would be the official record, and every state would have to run surprise hand-count audits of federal election results after each election. It also banned internet connections and wireless devices in vote-counting machines, required voting software to be deposited with an independent lab, let voters sue to enforce their right to a paper ballot, and sent $1 billion to states to replace noncompliant machines, with the audit costs federally reimbursed.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would gain a verifiable record of every vote: a paper ballot they could inspect before it counted, surprise post-election hand-count audits to catch errors or tampering, and the ability to sue in federal court if their right to a paper ballot was denied. Voters with disabilities, limited English, or literacy difficulties would be served by federally funded research into accessible paper-ballot verification. State and local election officials would get the federal money to pay for the transition — $1 billion for new equipment plus reimbursement of audit costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal election to use a durable paper ballot the voter can inspect and correct before casting, and makes that paper ballot the official record in any recount or audit, so a machine failure or software error cannot silently change results.

Requires every state to run surprise random hand-count audits of federal election results after each election — covering 3 to 10 percent of precincts depending on the margin of victory — and bars a state from certifying results until the audit is done and published.

Bans internet connections and wireless devices in vote-counting systems, requires voting software to be certified and held in escrow, and removes the Election Assistance Commission's exemption from federal contracting rules — the bill also required testing labs to be independent of the manufacturers whose equipment they approve.

Gives individual voters a private right of action: a person aggrieved by a violation of the voting-system requirements can file a complaint with the Attorney General or sue in federal court to enforce the right to a voter-verified paper ballot.

Funds the transition rather than pushing costs onto local governments: $1 billion for states to replace noncompliant machines (allocated toward the precincts that most need to replace equipment), payments covering audit costs, and grants to develop accessible voting methods for voters with disabilities, limited English, or literacy difficulties.

analysis.who_pays: The voting machine industry would bear the main cost: paperless touch-screen machines that record votes with no verifiable paper record could not be used in federal elections, forcing manufacturers to build and recertify compliant systems. Taxpayers generally would fund the $1 billion in state payments and roughly $100 million a year in audit reimbursements. Election administrators would face tighter procedures and faster deadlines on election night.

drawbacks.text: Hand-counting ballots in recounts and audits is slower and more labor-intensive than machine tallies, and the bill set tight timelines — audits had to begin within 24 hours of unofficial results, with a compressed effective date of November 2010 that would have strained states still buying equipment.

The bill authorized large new federal spending — $1 billion to replace noncompliant machines, $100 million a year to pay for audits, and research grants — a cost to taxpayers even though it was directed at states rather than households.

The bill would have overridden state procurement choices and required disclosure of voting-machine source code held in escrow, which vendors could reasonably object to on trade-secret grounds, even though the bill built in nondisclosure agreements to limit exposure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — every federal vote on a hand-countable paper ballot, with random audits and a legal way for voters to challenge failures — addresses a real weakness in election integrity, and the bill funded the transition rather than passing costs to local taxpayers. The drawbacks are real: hand-count audits are slower and more labor-intensive than machine tallies, the November 2010 start date left little time to buy and test new equipment, and the source-code disclosure rules would have drawn objections from voting technology makers on trade-secret grounds. On balance, a well-designed bill whose main cost was federal money and administrative effort, and whose failure left the pre-2009 voting systems in place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2009 and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson introduced the Voter Confidence and Increased Accessibility Act of 2009 in the Senate on July 9, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a single Senate Democrat, over its entire lifespan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of the paperless electronic voting machines in use at the time, who kept selling existing systems without the new requirements, and election officials who faced no change to their procedures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Paperless voting machine makers and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 9, 2009 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only two Democratic senators attached to the bill — the sponsor and one cosponsor — with no Republican support and no vote ever taken, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Voting machine and election technology vendors
industries.note: The bill would effectively have ended sales of paperless touch-screen machines, the vendors' flagship product, by requiring voter-verifiable paper ballots as the official record. At the same time, the $1 billion federal fund for replacing noncompliant equipment would have created a large new market for compliant optical-scan and ballot-marking systems, so vendors stood to lose one product line and gain another — but only after redesigning and recertifying their systems.

The bill required labs to be financially independent of the manufacturers they test and moved their compensation into an escrow account paid through the Election Assistance Commission, giving them steady, conflict-free funding. Independent testing serves voters' interest in certified equipment, so the industry's interest and the public's run together here.

They would have taken on new mandates — mandatory audits with 24-hour deadlines, paper ballots everywhere, machine bans — but the bill directed federal payments to cover both the equipment switch and the cost of each audit, and required states to reimburse local governments for compliance costs.

The bill authorized National Science Foundation grants to study accessible ballot verification and election-dedicated voting software, with any resulting technology treated as non-proprietary and made public.
